The Watsons came from the Clyde valley of Lanarkshire, Scotland’s cotton country.
William Watson was born at Dalserf about 1797 and Christina McGaan at Blantyre,
where the great cotton mill stood, about 1805.
They grew up in the weavers’ ruin: after the Napoleonic Wars the power loom took over,
hand-weavers’ wages collapsed, and in 1820 the west of Scotland came close to rising.
That year and the next, emigration societies took thousands of Lanarkshire weavers’ families to Upper Canada with
government help. William and Christina left a little later, in the early 1820s,
with their first child, and settled on the Trout River at Saint Anicet in Huntingdon County,
Lower Canada, where William was the first occupant of lot 45 in the 3rd Range; Christina’s sister and brother settled
nearby. The settlers there lived at first by lumbering and potash, and an old Saint Anicet man told the county historian
Robert Sellar that they took their grain to be ground by canoe, or on their backs,
to Fort Covington. It was border country.
Their son Alexander farmed at Elgin, a few miles from the New York line, and married Margaret Jane Moore,
who had come out from County Leitrim with her parents and brothers and sisters in the late 1860s,
Church of England Irish among the Scots.
